extracted.intended_audience: improv performers, teachers, and students (especially those studying Mick Napier's 'revisionist' approach)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical guidance for starting and developing an improvised scene from Mick Napier's 'Improvise: Scene from the Inside Out', emphasizing bold initiation, trusting instincts, specificity, and holding onto initial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do something at the top
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the performer do something at the top? ('At the top of an improv scene, in the first crucial moments, it is far more important that you do something than what it is you actually do.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiate an action immediately in the opening moments; the fact of taking action is more important than the particular content of that action. Avoid waiting for a 'perfect' opener or being idle at the start of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check out what you did
rubrics_metrics.description: Check out what you did — after taking action, notice and examine that action to see what it offers the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the implications and opportunities created by your initial move. Use 'checking out' to discover relationships, status, environment, or emotional stakes that can be pursued; this helps build the scene from the inside out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold onto the original choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Did they hold onto the original choice? / Hold onto it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and commit to your initial choice rather than abandoning or flip-flopping. Holding onto the original choice gives the scene a coherent throughline and makes developments richer and funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take care of yourself first (commit strongly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Did they take care of themselves (committed strongly)? / 'Take care of yourself first — then your scene partner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make choices that support your own clarity and commitment before prioritizing rescuing or protecting partners. Strong personal commitment grounds the scene and gives partners something solid to work with; avoid tentative or half-hearted offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust your first instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Did they trust their first instinct? / 'Trust your initial instinct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept and follow your immediate impulses instead of overthinking or second-guessing. First instincts are often the most useful and honest for establishing tone, character, and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity beats generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the choice specific? / 'Specificity beats generality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete, specific details (objects, names, actions, relationships) over vague or generic offers. Specific choices create clearer, funnier, and more playable realities for the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiate boldly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start scenes with confident, clear initiations rather than timid or uncertain openings. Bold initiations help define space, relationships, and stakes quickly and give partners strong material to react to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-think; commit
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid paralysis by analysis. Once a choice is made, commit to it fully rather than hesitating or trying to 'fix' it. Commitment amplifies choices and makes scene work more decisive and interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use improv 'rules' as corrective tools, not laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Rules' of improv (yes-and, no questions, etc.) were corrective responses to bad habits, not laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat common improv rules as guidelines to remedy specific problems rather than rigid constraints. Be willing to break or reinterpret rules if doing so serves the scene's truth and momentum.
